title: Cell Structure

# Cell Structure

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Identify the main components of animal and plant cells
- Describe the function of each cell organelle
- Explain why cells are considered the basic unit of life

## Introduction

All living organisms are made up of **cells** - the smallest unit of life. Cells were first discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665 when he observed cork under a microscope. The study of cells is called **cell biology** or **cytology**.

Cells are incredibly small - most are between 10-100 micrometres (μm) in diameter. Despite their tiny size, cells contain all the machinery needed for life processes.

## Key Concepts

### Cell Theory

The **cell theory** states that:
1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and organisation in organisms
3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells

### Common Cell Structures

All cells (both animal and plant) contain these essential structures:

#### Cell Membrane (Plasma Membrane)
- A thin, flexible barrier surrounding the cell
- Controls what enters and leaves the cell (selectively permeable)
- Made of a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins
- Approximately 7-8 nm thick

[DIAGRAM: Cell membrane structure showing phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins]

#### Cytoplasm
- A jelly-like substance filling the cell
- Contains water, salts, and organic molecules
- Where many chemical reactions occur (metabolic reactions)
- Contains the cytoskeleton - a network of protein fibres

#### Nucleus
- The control centre of the cell
- Contains genetic material (DNA) organised into chromosomes
- Surrounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope
- Contains the nucleolus, which produces ribosomes
- Controls cell activities by regulating gene expression

[DIAGRAM: Structure of the nucleus showing nuclear envelope, chromatin, and nucleolus]

#### Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion)
- The "powerhouse" of the cell
- Site of aerobic respiration
- Produces ATP (adenosine triphosphate) - the energy currency of cells
- Has a double membrane - inner membrane is folded into cristae
- Contains its own DNA (maternal inheritance)

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water} + \text{energy (ATP)}$$

[DIAGRAM: Mitochondrion showing outer membrane, inner membrane with cristae, and matrix]

#### Ribosomes
- Small structures where protein synthesis occurs
- Found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum
- Made of RNA and protein
- Read messenger RNA (mRNA) to build proteins
- Very small - approximately 20-30 nm in diameter

### Additional Organelles

#### Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)
**Rough ER:**
- Has ribosomes attached to its surface
- Produces proteins for export from the cell
- Continuous with the nuclear envelope

**Smooth ER:**
- No ribosomes attached
- Produces lipids and steroid hormones
- Involved in detoxification

#### Golgi Apparatus (Golgi Body)
- Stacks of flattened membrane sacs
- Modifies, packages, and distributes proteins
- Produces lysosomes
- Adds carbohydrates to proteins (glycosylation)

[DIAGRAM: Golgi apparatus showing cisternae and vesicles]

#### Lysosomes
- Contain digestive enzymes
- Break down worn-out organelles
- Digest materials taken in by the cell
- Important for the immune response

## Practical Applications

### Why Understanding Cell Structure Matters

1. **Medicine:** Many diseases occur at the cellular level. Understanding cell structure helps develop treatments for cancer, genetic disorders, and infections.

2. **Biotechnology:** Knowledge of cell components allows scientists to modify cells for producing medicines like insulin.

3. **Forensics:** Cell analysis helps identify individuals through DNA found in cell nuclei.

## Common Exam Questions

- Describe the function of the nucleus/mitochondria/cell membrane
- Explain why cells need mitochondria
- Compare the structure and function of rough and smooth ER
- State the functions of three named organelles

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** The cell membrane is rigid and solid
- **Reality:** The cell membrane is fluid and flexible, often described by the "fluid mosaic model"

- **Misconception:** All cells are the same size and shape
- **Reality:** Cells vary enormously in size (from 1 μm bacteria to 30 cm nerve cells) and shape depending on their function

- **Misconception:** The nucleus stores energy
- **Reality:** The nucleus contains DNA and controls cell activities; mitochondria produce energy

## Practice Questions

1. Name the organelle responsible for producing ATP. (1 mark)

2. State two functions of the cell membrane. (2 marks)

3. Explain why cells contain mitochondria. (2 marks)

4. A student observes a cell under a microscope. They can see a nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes, but no cell wall. What type of cell is this likely to be? Explain your answer. (3 marks)

5. Describe the structure and function of the Golgi apparatus. (4 marks)

6. Explain how the structure of the mitochondrion is related to its function. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Cell | The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms |
| Cell membrane | A selectively permeable barrier controlling entry and exit of substances |
| Cytoplasm | Jelly-like substance where metabolic reactions occur |
| Nucleus | Control centre containing DNA |
| Mitochondria | Organelles that carry out aerobic respiration to produce ATP |
| Ribosomes | Small structures where protein synthesis occurs |
| Organelle | A specialised structure within a cell with a specific function |
| ATP | Adenosine triphosphate - the energy currency of cells |

## Summary

- Cells are the basic unit of life, first described by cell theory
- All cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and genetic material
- The nucleus contains DNA and controls cell activities
- Mitochondria produce ATP through aerobic respiration
- Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis
- Each organelle has a specific structure suited to its function
